content: Risedronate is prescribed to prevent and treat osteoporosis, a condition characterized by thinning and weakening of bones that can lead to fractures. It is specifically used in postmenopausal women, men, and individuals taking glucocorticoids (a type of medication that can cause osteoporosis). Additionally, it is used to treat Paget's disease of bone, a condition where bones become soft, weak, deformed, painful, or prone to fractures. Risedronate belongs to a class of medications called bisphosphonates, which work by preventing bone breakdown and increasing bone density. Risedronate is available as an oral tablet and is typically taken on an empty stomach, either once daily in the morning or once weekly on the same day each week. It is crucial to follow the prescription instructions exactly as directed. Taking more or less than prescribed, or not adhering to the instructions, may reduce the medication's effectiveness and cause damage to the esophagus or mouth sores. To ensure proper use: Take risedronate immediately after getting out of bed in the morning, before eating or drinking anything. Do not take it at bedtime or before getting out of bed. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass (6–8 ounces) of plain water while sitting or standing upright. Do not take it with tea, coffee, juice, mineral water, milk, or any liquid other than plain water. Do not split, chew, crush, or suck on the tablets. Avoid holding the tablet in your mouth for any length of time. After taking risedronate, do not eat, drink, or take any other medications for at least 30 minutes. Remain upright (sitting or standing) for at least 30 minutes after taking the medication. Risedronate helps manage osteoporosis and Paget's disease but does not cure these conditions. It is effective only when taken regularly. Continue taking it even if you feel well, and do not stop without consulting your doctor. If you miss a dose: For once-daily dosing, skip the missed dose and take the next dose the following morning as usual. Do not take it later in the day. For once-weekly dosing, take the missed dose the morning after you remember, then return to your regular schedule. Do not take more than one dose in a single day or double up to make up for a missed dose. Risedronate may cause mild side effects, such as nausea, burping, dry mouth, stomach pain, diarrhea, constipation, gas, headache, dizziness, depression, anxiety, weakness, leg cramps, bone/joint/muscle pain, back pain, flu-like symptoms, fever, chills, sore throat, cough, frequent or painful urination, runny nose, dry eyes, or ringing in the ears. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Serious side effects include difficulty swallowing, new or worsening heartburn, chest pain, bloody vomit, vomit resembling coffee grounds, black or bloody stools, itching, rash, hives, skin blisters, swelling of the face/throat/tongue/lips/eyes/hands/feet/ankles/lower legs, difficulty breathing, hoarseness, red or painful eyes, or sensitivity to light. If you experience any of these, stop taking risedronate and contact your doctor immediately. Store risedronate in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, give the person a full glass of milk and contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the person collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include numbness or tingling around the mouth or in the hands/feet, muscle spasms, cramps, twitches, or seizures. Before starting risedronate, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it or any other medications, and provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Mention any history of low blood calcium, difficulty sitting or standing upright for 30 minutes, swallowing problems, heartburn, ulcers, stomach/esophagus issues, anemia, cancer, infections (especially in the mouth), dental problems, blood clotting disorders, or kidney disease. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning to become pregnant, as risedronate may remain in your body for years after stopping it. Risedronate may cause serious jaw problems, especially if you undergo dental surgery or treatment while taking it. Have a dentist examine your teeth and perform any necessary treatments before starting risedronate. Maintain good oral hygiene and consult your doctor before undergoing any dental procedures while on this medication. To prevent osteoporosis, your doctor may recommend avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol consumption, and engaging in regular weight-bearing exercise. Additionally, consume foods rich in calcium and vitamin D, or take supplements if needed, as advised by your doctor. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory for monitoring. Inform healthcare providers that you are taking risedronate before undergoing any tests or imaging studies. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refilling your prescription.
